The film centers on Carl, an ill-tempered elderly man, who struggles to deal with the boundless energy of a young boy named Russell. Now, there's certainly no problem with an animated movie pulling at our heartstrings. Yet you can almost feel a wave of discomfort spreading among the youngest members of the family audience when, roughly five minutes into an energetic opening sequence, the adventurous youngsters Carl and Ellie suddenly transform into a married couple, and soon after, a long-married one. Right before our eyes, they age and hunch over, exchanging their childhood ambitions of adventure for the quiet contentment of home life. Ellie longs for a child but is unable to conceive. The money they've set aside for their dream getaway keeps getting drained by one unexpected expense after another, one household calamity after the next, until their time together simply runs out -- at least, for Ellie.

That leaves us alone with Carl, a cantankerous stay-at-home type voiced by Ed Asner, whose silence makes WALL-E seem downright talkative. And keep in mind, he's one of our leading characters. Sure, nobody was openly asking when the dancing penguins would appear, but I'd bet the thought crossed someone's mind. Watch a preview of "Up" ».

Those doubts, however, prove unwarranted. When it comes to spectacle, "Up" absolutely delivers. Perhaps not penguins, exactly, but far more than the flying house shown in the advertisements. There's a legendary, rainbow-hued bird -- possibly a snipe, possibly not -- who goes by the name Kevin and has developed quite a fondness for chocolate bars. There are airships, old-fashioned adventurers, and talking dogs -- an entire pack of them, actually. These are dogs that pour wine, deal cards, and pilot biplanes. And then there's Russell, a plump little Boy Scout -- or "Wilderness Explorer" -- who shows up at Carl's door at the most inconvenient moment. You see, Carl craves freedom, and to achieve it, he sends his house soaring into the heavens using thousands of balloons. How could he have possibly known Russell was on board?

That said, "Up" doesn't stay airborne the whole time. The dogs' comedic antics feel more like something out of "Beverly Hills Chihuahua" than what we're accustomed to from Pixar, a studio that usually doesn't bend the rules of reality just to score a few easy chuckles. # The Emotional Heights of Pixar's "Up"

The film "Up" opens with an emotionally heavy prologue that follows Carl and Ellie from their youth through marriage and ultimately to Ellie's death. This poignant montage traces the arc of an entire life together—the shared dreams, the quiet disappointments, and the enduring love between two people. By beginning with such a tender and ultimately sorrowful sequence, the movie establishes a decidedly somber tone that sets it apart from typical animated fare.

After losing his wife, Carl becomes a grumpy, quiet homebody. Voiced with gruff warmth by Ed Asner, the elderly widower has retreated into isolation, clinging to the home he once shared with Ellie and the memories it holds. His solitary existence is unexpectedly disrupted when he is joined by Russell, an enthusiastic young Boy Scout whose boundless energy and eagerness stand in sharp contrast to Carl's withdrawn demeanor. This unlikely pairing forms the emotional heart of the story.

Despite its melancholy beginning, the movie delivers plenty of spectacle. Carl's house, lifted into the sky by thousands of colorful balloons, becomes the vehicle for a grand adventure. Along the way, the film introduces soaring zeppelins and the lingering legends of old-time explorers, filling the screen with a sense of wonder and grand ambition that balances the story's more introspective moments.

The film also features an array of whimsical characters that add charm and humor to the journey. Among them is Kevin, a mythical multicolored bird with an unlikely fondness for candy bars, whose exotic appearance and playful behavior provide both comedy and warmth. Equally memorable is a pack of talking dogs, outfitted with special collars that give them voices, who fly biplanes and gather to play cards—delightfully absurd touches that expand the film's imaginative world.

While "Up" is largely successful, some elements fall short of the film's otherwise high standard. The dogs' comedic antics, in particular, occasionally feel out of step with the movie's more sophisticated tone, evoking the broad, lowbrow humor of lesser films such as "Beverly Hills Chihuahua." These moments, though minor, slightly undercut the emotional and visual achievements that make the film so remarkable overall.

"Up," Pixar's 10th feature-length film, tells the story of Carl Fredricksen, a grumpy senior citizen who launches his house into the sky using thousands of balloons, and Russell, an enthusiastic young Boy Scout who unexpectedly joins his journey.

The film opens with a prologue that is remarkable for its emotional depth. We meet Carl as a shy young boy, watch him fall in love with the adventurous Ellie, and follow their life together through decades of shared dreams and quiet disappointments. This montage, which unfolds without dialogue, culminates in Ellie's death, leaving Carl a widower who has lost his sense of purpose. It is a melancholy beginning, one that sets a surprisingly somber tone for what audiences might expect to be a lighthearted animated adventure.

When developers threaten to force him from the home he shared with Ellie, Carl takes drastic action. Rather than surrender to a retirement facility, he ties thousands of colorful balloons to his house and lifts off, intent on fulfilling a lifelong promise to reach Paradise Falls in South America. What he doesn't anticipate is a stowaway: Russell, the eager young Boy Scout who had knocked on his door earlier, now clinging to the porch as the house sails away.

From here, the film transforms into an imaginative spectacle. Carl and Russell's journey introduces them to a fantastical world filled with wonders, including a mythical bird that Russell names Kevin, packs of talking dogs equipped with special collars that translate their thoughts into speech, and looming zeppelins that add grandeur and menace to the adventure.

# 'Up' Soars as Pixar's Most Heartfelt Adventure Yet

*A CNN Entertainment Review*

Pixar Animation Studios has done it again — and this time, they've reached altitudes both literal and emotional that few animated films dare to attempt.

## A Story That Takes Flight

"Up" follows Carl Fredricksen, a 78-year-old balloon salesman whose life has been defined by an unfulfilled promise. After the loss of his beloved wife Ellie — depicted in a wordless opening montage that ranks among the most devastatingly beautiful sequences in film history — Carl decides to fulfill their shared dream. He attaches thousands of helium balloons to his house and sets off for Paradise Falls in South America.

The catch? He's inadvertently brought along a stowaway: Russell, an earnest young Wilderness Explorer determined to earn his final merit badge. What begins as an old man's solitary pilgrimage becomes an unexpected odyssey involving a rare tropical bird, a pack of talking dogs, and a childhood hero harboring dark secrets.

## Characters With Genuine Heart

Carl, voiced with gruff tenderness by Ed Asner, is a revelation — a curmudgeonly protagonist whose emotional armor slowly cracks to reveal the wounded romantic beneath. It's rare for any film, let alone an animated one, to center on an elderly widower and make audiences care so deeply.

Young Russell provides both comic relief and emotional counterweight, while the scene-stealing Dug the dog — equipped with a collar that translates his thoughts — delivers some of the film's biggest laughs. ("Squirrel!")

## Visual Splendor

Pixar's animation continues to push boundaries. The floating house, buoyed by its rainbow canopy of balloons, is rendered with breathtaking detail. The lush landscapes of Paradise Falls burst with color and dimension, and the character animation captures nuanced emotion in every wrinkle and glance.

## The Verdict

"Up" is that rare family film that respects its youngest viewers while speaking profoundly to adults about love, loss, aging, and the courage to embrace new adventures. It's funny, thrilling, and — be warned — a genuine tearjerker.

**Rating: 4.5 out of 5 stars**

Pixar hasn't just made another great animated film. They've crafted a meditation on life itself that will leave audiences of all ages floating on air.

# Up (2009): A Soaring Achievement in Animated Storytelling

Pixar's *Up*, directed by Pete Docter, stands as one of the studio's most emotionally ambitious films—a work that dares to open with heartbreak before lifting us, quite literally, into an adventure of joy, grief, and unexpected connection.

## The Opening Montage: Four Minutes That Redefined Animation

It's impossible to discuss *Up* without dwelling on its opening sequence, "Married Life." In roughly four dialogue-free minutes, Docter and his team chronicle the entire relationship of Carl and Ellie Fredricksen—from their childhood meeting as adventure-obsessed kids through marriage, the quiet devastation of infertility, the accumulation of a shared life, and finally Ellie's death.

What makes this montage extraordinary is its restraint. Michael Giacchino's Oscar-winning score does emotional heavy lifting through a single recurring theme that shifts between playful and mournful. The sequence trusts its audience to read faces, gestures, and small moments—Carl straightening Ellie's tie, the empty chair, the recurring image of them saving coins in a jar only to break it for emergencies. It's storytelling at its most economical and devastating, and it has become a benchmark against which emotional animation is measured. Few films, animated or live-action, achieve this much in so little time.

## Carl and Russell: An Odd Couple Worth Rooting For

The heart of the film lies in the reluctant partnership between Carl, a curmudgeonly 78-year-old widower, and Russell, an earnest, overeager Wilderness Explorer desperate for his final merit badge. On paper, it's a familiar odd-couple dynamic, but the film earns genuine warmth from it.

Carl's grief has calcified into stubbornness—his journey to Paradise Falls is really an act of devotion to Ellie's unfulfilled dream. Russell, meanwhile, carries his own quiet sadness, hinting at an absent father who's stopped showing up. Their bond develops not through forced sentimentality but through shared danger and small kindnesses. The gradual thaw in Carl—choosing Russell and a life of new purpose over the literal weight of his old house—provides the film's emotional throughline and its ultimate message: adventure isn't found in exotic locations, but in the people we choose to care for.

## The Talking Dogs: Comic Relief With a Catch

Then there's Dug and his pack. Equipped with collars that translate their thoughts into speech, the dogs provide much of the film's comedy. Dug, the lovable golden retriever who instantly adopts Carl and Russell ("I have just met you, and I love you"), is a delight—capturing canine loyalty and distractibility with the immortal "SQUIRREL!" gag.

The dogs are where *Up* leans hardest into broad comedy, and opinions vary on whether this tonal shift works. After the film's grounded emotional opening, the villainous Alpha and his squadron of aviator dogs push the story into more conventional adventure-movie territory. Some viewers find this a jarring pivot; others appreciate the levity as necessary counterbalance to the heavier themes. Personally, I find the dogs charming enough to forgive the tonal whiplash, even if they represent the film's most cartoonish elements.

## Does It Live Up to Pixar's Standards?

Emphatically, yes—though not without minor caveats. *Up* arrived during Pixar's remarkable golden run (bookended by *Ratatouille*, *WALL-E*, and *Toy Story 3*), and it holds its own among that company. Its greatest strength is thematic maturity: this is a film willing to explore aging, loss, and the danger of living in the past, subjects rarely centered in family entertainment.

The third act, involving the villainous explorer Charles Muntz and a rescued exotic bird named Kevin, is more standard adventure fare and doesn't quite match the transcendence of the opening. But this is a common Pixar pattern—setting a bar so impossibly high early on that the rest of the film can only approach, not exceed it.

**Verdict:** *Up* is a beautiful, moving, and visually gorgeous film that showcases Pixar at the height of its powers. It's a story about learning to let go of grief and finding new reasons to live, wrapped in the guise of a colorful balloon adventure. Its imperfect back half is more than redeemed by an opening that ranks among the finest sequences in animation history.

**Rating: 4.5 / 5**

# Up: Pixar's Soaring Meditation on Life, Loss, and Second Chances

**Rating: PG | Runtime: 96 minutes**

## A Story That Floats Above Expectations

Don't let the opening fool you. The first ten minutes of Pixar's *Up* might rank among the most heartbreaking sequences ever committed to animation—a wordless montage chronicling a lifetime of love, disappointment, and profound loss that leaves few adult viewers dry-eyed. You'd be forgiven for wondering how a children's film could open on such a melancholy note. But this is precisely the genius of *Up*: it grounds you in grief only to lift you, quite literally, into the skies of wonder.

## Characters Worth the Journey

At the heart of the film is Carl Fredricksen, a 78-year-old widower voiced with gruff tenderness by Ed Asner. Carl is no conventional hero. He's stubborn, curmudgeonly, and weighed down by regret over a shared dream he never fulfilled with his late wife, Ellie. When developers threaten his beloved home, Carl does the unthinkable—he ties thousands of balloons to his house and sets sail for the wilds of South America.

He doesn't travel alone. Russell, an earnest and endlessly chatty young Wilderness Explorer, becomes his unlikely stowaway. The dynamic between the grumbling old man and the irrepressibly optimistic boy forms the emotional spine of the story. Their relationship evolves organically, each filling a void in the other's life. Add a lovable, misunderstood giant bird named Kevin and Dug, a golden retriever with a talking collar and impeccable comedic timing, and you have an ensemble that balances heartbreak with genuine joy.

## Adventure at Ten Thousand Feet

Once the house takes flight, *Up* transforms into a rollicking adventure. Director Pete Docter crafts a visually stunning world of towering cliffs, mysterious jungles, and the fabled Paradise Falls. The animation is breathtaking, with the floating house serving as both a whimsical vehicle and a poignant symbol of the past Carl refuses to release.

The film delivers thrilling set pieces—airship battles, dangerous cliffside chases, and encounters with a menacing explorer voiced by Christopher Plummer. Yet the adventure never overshadows the emotional core. Every action beat serves the deeper story of a man learning to let go and embrace the life still ahead of him.

## The Verdict

*Up* is a rare cinematic achievement that speaks to audiences of all ages on entirely different levels. Children will delight in the talking dogs and soaring balloons, while adults will find themselves moved by its meditation on marriage, mortality, and the courage it takes to begin again.

This is Pixar operating at the height of its powers—technically dazzling, emotionally resonant, and profoundly humane. What begins as a story about endings becomes, beautifully, a story about beginnings.

**Highly recommended.** Bring tissues for the opening, and stay for the uplifting journey that follows. *Up* earns its place among the finest animated films ever made.

# 'Up' Soars on Emotion, Even When Its Story Drifts

**A Pixar triumph of heart and imagination that occasionally struggles under the weight of its own ambitions**

Pixar's tenth feature film opens with what may be the most emotionally devastating four minutes in the studio's history—and possibly in modern American animation. The wordless montage chronicling the marriage of Carl and Ellie Fredricksen, from childhood sweethearts to a lifetime of shared dreams deferred and ultimately unrealized, is a masterclass in visual storytelling. By the time we watch an elderly Carl sitting alone after Ellie's death, "Up" has already earned its place among cinema's most affecting portraits of love and loss.

That the rest of the film cannot quite sustain this staggering opening is both its central weakness and, perhaps, an unfair standard by which to measure it.

## A Premise That Takes Flight

The story that follows is pure whimsy: Carl, a curmudgeonly 78-year-old widower voiced with gruff tenderness by Ed Asner, ties thousands of balloons to his house and sails toward the South American wilderness his late wife always dreamed of visiting. It's a premise that shouldn't work—and in the hands of a lesser studio, wouldn't—yet director Pete Docter grounds the fantastical in genuine emotional truth.

Carl's unlikely stowaway, an earnest young Wilderness Explorer named Russell, provides both comic relief and the film's beating heart. Their odd-couple dynamic drives the narrative, and young Jordan Nagai brings an authentic, unpolished energy to Russell that never tips into cloying territory.

## Where the Adventure Falters

Here the film's ambitions begin to strain. Once Carl and Russell reach their destination, "Up" pivots into more conventional adventure-movie territory, complete with a talking dog, an exotic bird named Kevin, and a villain—famed explorer Charles Muntz—whose motivations feel thinly sketched compared to the rich interior lives established in the film's opening act.

The talking dogs, equipped with translation collars, deliver genuine laughs ("Squirrel!" has rightly entered the cultural lexicon), but they also represent a tonal shift toward broader comedy that sits uneasily beside the film's meditation on grief. The third-act action sequences, while technically dazzling, occasionally feel obligatory—as though the film must deliver spectacle to justify its runtime, even when its truest spectacle is emotional.

## A Visual Marvel

Visually, "Up" is a wonder. The floating house, buoyed by a rainbow canopy of balloons, is an indelible image, and the lush, exaggerated landscapes of Paradise Falls showcase Pixar's continued technical supremacy. The animators' attention to detail—the way Carl grips his walker, the physical comedy of aging bodies in motion—reveals a studio at the height of its craft.

Michael Giacchino's Oscar-winning score deserves particular praise, weaving Carl and Ellie's theme throughout the film in ways that consistently earn its emotional payoffs.

## The Verdict

"Up" is not a perfect film. Its narrative sags in the middle, its antagonist underwhelms, and it never fully reconciles the profound melancholy of its opening with the cartoonish adventure that follows. But these flaws feel almost churlish to dwell upon when weighed against what the film achieves.

This is a movie unafraid to explore mortality, regret, and the quiet heroism of moving forward after loss—themes rarely broached in family entertainment. That it does so while remaining genuinely funny and visually spectacular is a testament to Pixar's singular ability to trust its audience, young and old.

"Up" may not fly as high in its second half as it does in its first, but even a grounded Pixar film soars above most of its competition.

**Rating: 3.5 out of 4 stars**

# "Up": Pixar Soars to New Emotional Heights

Pixar Animation Studios has built its reputation on films that appeal to children while resonating deeply with adults, but "Up" may be the studio's most ambitious emotional gambit yet. This is a film that opens with a montage so achingly beautiful and profoundly sad that it dares its young audience to keep up—and then rewards everyone with an adventure of genuine wonder and heart.

## A Grumpy Hero Worth Rooting For

At the center of it all is Carl Fredricksen, a 78-year-old widower brought to life by the incomparable **Ed Asner**. Asner's gravelly, curmudgeonly voice is nothing short of perfect casting. He imbues Carl with just the right blend of stubbornness, grief, and buried tenderness. When Carl grumbles and grouses, Asner makes us laugh; when the character's loneliness peeks through, that same voice breaks our hearts. It's a masterclass in vocal performance, proving that great acting doesn't require a face on screen—only the truth in a voice.

Carl's grand plan is to fulfill a lifelong dream he shared with his late wife, Ellie: to relocate his entire house to the wilds of South America by tying thousands of helium balloons to it. His destination is **Paradise Falls**, the mythic tabletop mountain locale that represents everything he and Ellie once promised each other. The film renders Paradise Falls with breathtaking artistry—all misty cliffs, lush jungle, and cascading water that feels like a lost world torn from an old adventure serial.

## An Unlikely Companion

Carl doesn't get to fly solo, however. Enter **Russell**, an earnest, overeager **Wilderness Explorer** who stows away on the floating house in pursuit of his final merit badge—the one for "Assisting the Elderly." Russell is a delightful creation: chubby, breathless, endlessly chattering, and utterly guileless. His relentless optimism serves as the perfect foil to Carl's sourness, and the gradual thawing of their relationship forms the film's beating heart. Russell isn't just comic relief; he carries his own quiet sadness, a subplot handled with the restraint and grace that distinguishes Pixar's best work.

## Feathers and Fur

The South American wilderness introduces a menagerie of memorable characters, chief among them **Kevin**, a gangly, iridescent, twelve-foot-tall flightless bird. Kevin is a triumph of animation—all awkward limbs and vivid plumage—and the running gag of "her" true identity provides genuine laughs. There's also Dug, a golden retriever whose thoughts are broadcast through a special collar, delivering some of the film's most quotable moments ("Squirrel!"). Together, this ragtag group transforms Carl's solitary pilgrimage into a full-fledged rescue adventure.

## The 3-D Question

Much has been made of the film's **3-D presentation**, and it deserves comment. Unlike the gimmicky, in-your-face 3-D of lesser productions, "Up" uses the technology with tasteful subtlety. Rather than hurling objects at the audience, the added dimension enhances depth—the vertiginous drop from a cliff's edge, the layered floating of countless balloons, the vast expanse of sky. It deepens immersion without ever distracting from the storytelling. That said, the film is so beautifully composed and emotionally rich that it loses none of its power in standard 2-D. The 3-D is a lovely enhancement, not a necessity.

## Final Verdict

"Up" is a remarkable achievement, a film that balances slapstick comedy and swashbuckling adventure with meditations on grief, aging, and the promises we make to those we love. It trusts its audience—young and old alike—to sit with genuine emotion, and it rewards that trust with an ending as uplifting as its premise suggests. Anchored by Ed Asner's superb voice work and populated with unforgettable characters, this is Pixar operating at the peak of its considerable powers.

**★★★★½ out of five**

A soaring triumph of imagination and heart. Bring tissues.
